title: Gillispie v. Goodyear Service Stores
lead: Hilda Calahan Gillispie accused several defendants of entering her home, assaulting her, and causing her confinement. Her complaint supplied legal labels and dates but little account of who did what, prompting a dispute over the facts required by North Carolina’s code pleading system.

actors.name: Hilda Calahan Gillispie
actors.role: Plaintiff seeking actual and punitive damages for alleged tortious conduct.

actors.name: Goodyear Service Stores, its corporate parent, and four individuals
actors.role: Defendants whose concrete roles in the alleged incident were not explained in the complaint.

actors.name: Judge Mintz
actors.role: Trial judge who sustained the demurrers with leave to amend.

proceedings: The trial court sustained four demurrers and allowed thirty days to amend. The North Carolina Supreme Court affirmed for failure to state a cause of action, rejected misjoinder as the basis, and preserved the opportunity to amend.
limits: This is a historical code-pleading decision, not a merits finding or an account of current North Carolina rules. The report gives dates despite the opinion’s later criticism that the complaint failed to disclose when the events occurred; that textual tension remains explicit.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: The complaint alleges serious misconduct without explaining the incident
paragraphs: Hilda Calahan Gillispie alleged that on or about May 5 and 6, 1959, Goodyear Service Stores, its corporate parent, and four individuals maliciously entered her residence, used threatening language and physical force, assaulted and frightened her, exposed her to public ridicule, and caused her seizure and confinement in jail. These were accusations, not established events.

Gillispie sued those defendants for $25,000 in actual damages and $10,000 in punitive damages. Her complaint identified the individuals as Alamance County residents and described the company's Burlington store and its division, but did not explain the participants' concrete relationships or the circumstances underlying the alleged wrongs.

sections.title: Four demurrers raise both factual sufficiency and joinder
sections.cue: Why did the permission to amend matter on appeal?
paragraphs: The defendants filed four separate demurrers challenging the factual allegations and the joinder of parties and causes of action. Judge Mintz entered a separate judgment sustaining each, without specifying the ground, and allowed Gillispie thirty days to amend. She appealed all four judgments.

Justice Bobbitt first addressed that ambiguity. A judgment sustaining a demurrer for misjoinder would require dismissal, so leave to amend suggested reliance on failure to state a cause of action. Independently, the allegations did not show misjoinder: even if they described multiple wrongs, they accused every defendant of participating in all of them. The Supreme Court therefore did not uphold a dismissal for improper joinder.

sections.title: The code requires ultimate facts to which law can be applied
sections.cue: What distinguished an allegation from a legal conclusion?
paragraphs: The governing statute required a plain and concise statement of the facts constituting the cause of action. The Court understood that to mean material, essential, ultimate facts establishing a right to relief, rather than the pleader’s conclusions. A demurrer admitted pleaded facts for purposes of the challenge, but did not admit legal conclusions.

The standard also favored preserving a complaint unless fatally defective. If any part supplied facts constituting a cause of action, the pleading would stand. For a tort, however, there still had to be facts showing a duty, breach, and resulting injury.

The opinion illustrated the distinction with other subjects. Saying a defendant owed money did not explain the source of the debt; calling an injury negligent did not identify the conduct or causal connection. Those examples explained the rule rather than recharacterizing Gillispie’s case. A judge needed to know the actual asserted wrong to determine admissible evidence, issues for trial, and the charge.

sections.title: The legal labels leave the operative conduct unexplained
sections.cue: What was missing even under a favorable reading?
paragraphs: The Court regarded the single sentence alleging trespass, assault, and confinement as conclusions lacking an adequate factual foundation. The complaint did not explain the occasion, identify who committed which acts, or connect the parties through concrete relationships.

The opinion also said the complaint did not disclose when the events occurred, although the reported pleading itself supplied the May 1959 dates. That discrepancy does not erase the dates. The central identified deficiency was the absence of an account underlying the legal labels.

Even the most favorable construction, the Court concluded, supplied no sufficient facts to which law could be applied. Earlier decisions treating an unexplained assertion of assault as a conclusion supported that result. A recovery had to rest on the case actually pleaded.

sections.title: Affirmance leaves Gillispie an opportunity to plead again
paragraphs: On January 11, 1963, the North Carolina Supreme Court affirmed the four judgments for failure to state a cause of action. It said amendment under the existing leave would be appropriate. It did not decide that the alleged misconduct never happened, award damages, or require dismissal for misjoinder.

Bobbitt wrote the sole reported opinion. The report provides no separate writing or numerical voting statement. Gillispie’s remaining opportunity was to amend the deficient account, not an adjudicated victory or defeat on the truth of the underlying accusations.
